title: Malo vs Mal: Bad or Badly in Spanish?

meta_description: Malo vs mal: malo is the adjective bad, mal the adverb badly and the short form before nouns. Estar mal, ser malo, caer mal, common mistakes and a quiz.

body_html:
Malo vs mal works like {{link:bueno-vs-bien|bueno vs bien}}: malo is the adjective “bad”, and mal is the adverb “badly”. But mal has a second job: it is also the short form of malo before a masculine singular noun, as in un mal día. Add the meanings of estar malo (to be ill or taste bad) and caer mal (to dislike someone), and you have everything you need.

Quick answer
  • Malo / mala / malos / malas = bad (adjective): una mala idea.
  • Mal = badly (adverb): Duermo mal.
  • Mal = bad, before a masculine singular noun: un mal momento.
  • Estoy mal = I’m not well; estoy malo = I’m ill (Spain).
{{toc}}

Malo vs mal: the core rule

MaloMal
Part of speechAdjectiveAdverb (and short adjective)
DescribesNounsVerbs; masculine singular nouns when placed before them
Changes form?Yes: malo, mala, malos, malasNo
ExampleEs una película mala.Canta muy mal. / Fue un mal año.

The RAE dictionary notes that malo shortens to mal before a masculine singular noun.

Malo: describing nouns

  • Es un hombre malo. He’s a bad (wicked) man.
  • Tengo malas noticias. I have bad news.
  • Esta fruta es mala para el perro. This fruit is bad for the dog.
  • Soy malo para los nombres. I’m bad with names.

Mal: describing actions and states

  • Hoy he dormido mal. I slept badly today.
  • Me siento mal. I feel bad / unwell.
  • Lo hice mal. I did it wrong.
  • Huele mal. It smells bad.

Note huele mal and sabe mal: Spanish describes how something smells or tastes with the adverb.

{{image:2}}

Mal before a noun

Before a masculine singular noun, malo drops the -o: un mal día, un mal ejemplo, mal humor. Feminine and plural forms don’t shorten: una mala noche, malos recuerdos. After the noun, use the full form: un día malo.

Ser malo, estar malo, estar mal

PhraseMeaningExample
ser maloto be bad (character, quality)Ese perro no es malo. That dog isn’t vicious.
estar maloto be ill (Spain); to taste badEstoy malo, tengo fiebre. / La leche está mala.
estar malto be unwell, wrong, not okayEstá mal mentir. It’s wrong to lie.

The ser/estar contrast is explained in {{link:ser-vs-estar|ser vs estar}}.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Useful expressions with mal

  • Me cae mal. I don’t like him/her (as a person).
  • Menos mal. Thank goodness / Just as well.
  • No está mal. Not bad.
  • Salir mal. To go wrong: El examen me salió mal.
  • Tomarse algo a mal. To take something the wrong way.
  • Ir de mal en peor. To go from bad to worse.

Why this pair is tricky for learners

English often uses “bad” where grammar would expect “badly”: “I feel bad”, “it smells bad”. Spanish keeps the adverb in these cases, so learners say me siento malo or huele malo. Then the short form mal before nouns makes it look as if the adverb is describing a noun. The fix is to remember two contexts for mal: after a verb, and right before a masculine singular noun. Everywhere else, use malo with agreement.

Real conversation

  • A: ¿Qué tal la entrevista? (How was the interview?)
  • B: Mal. Me puse nervioso y respondí fatal. ¡Qué mal día! (Badly. I got nervous and answered terribly. What a bad day!)
  • A: Bueno, no te lo tomes a mal, pero seguro que no fue tan malo. (Well, don’t take this the wrong way, but I’m sure it wasn’t that bad.)

Regional notes

In Spain, estoy malo or estoy mala is the everyday way to say you are ill: Mi hijo está malo y no va al cole. In most of Latin America, people say estoy enfermo instead, and estoy malo may sound odd. Everywhere, estoy mal means you are not well, physically or emotionally. Another regional favorite is fatal, very common in Spain as a stronger “badly”: Lo pasé fatal (I had an awful time), Cocino fatal (I’m a terrible cook).

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Me siento malo.Me siento mal.After sentirse: adverb
un malo díaun mal díaShort form before masculine nouns
una mal ideauna mala ideaFeminine doesn’t shorten
Huele malo.Huele mal.Adverb with oler
Tengo mal noticias.Tengo malas noticias.Plural adjective
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. It was a bad year. (Fue un mal año.)
  2. She drives badly. (Maneja mal.)
  3. I don’t like your friend. (Tu amigo me cae mal.)
  4. That’s a bad idea. (Es una mala idea.)
  5. Thank goodness you came! (¡Menos mal que viniste!)

The same logic explains {{link:muy-vs-mucho|muy vs mucho}}. More pairs in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

After a verb: mal. Before a masculine singular noun: mal. Everywhere else, describing a noun: malo, mala, malos, malas. And when someone asks how you are and things aren’t great, the answer is estoy mal, never estoy malo unless you have a fever in Spain.

faq.q: What is the difference between malo and mal?
faq.a: Malo is an adjective meaning bad and agrees with the noun. Mal is an adverb meaning badly, and also the short form of malo before a masculine singular noun (un mal día).

faq.q: Is it me siento mal or me siento malo?
faq.a: Me siento mal. After sentirse, Spanish uses the adverb mal.

faq.q: What does me cae mal mean?
faq.a: It means you don’t like someone as a person: Ese chico me cae mal (I don’t like that guy).
